name: Chang'e 1
short_status: Controlled impact in Mare Fecunditatis Mar 1, 2009, 08:13 UTC, after 16 months in orbit; the impact scar was later identified in LROC images at 1.66 S, 52.27 E (Icarus, 2019).
tagline: CNSA · China · Orbiter · 2007 · The quiet decades Success
stats: in lunar orbit, four beyond the one-year design life
resolution of China's first full-Moon image map
raw science data returned from eight instruments
mission cost, about 180 million dollars in 2007

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 24 October 2007, 10:05 UTC, Long March 3A from Launch Complex 3, Xichang Satellite Launch Center

facts.label: Spacecraft
facts.value: Built on the DFH-3 communications-satellite bus; 2,350 kg at launch, 1,150 kg dry

facts.label: Working orbit
facts.value: 200 km circular polar orbit, 127-minute period; captured 5 November 2007, final circularization November 7

facts.label: First for China
facts.value: China's first spacecraft to depart Earth orbit; only the USSR/Russia, the US, ESA and Japan had flown lunar missions before

facts.label: Science payload
facts.value: Eight instruments, about 140 kg: CCD stereo camera (120 m, 60 km swath), laser altimeter, imaging interferometer spectrometer, gamma-ray and X-ray spectrometers, microwave radiometer, high-energy particle detector, two solar wind ion detectors

facts.label: Microwave first
facts.value: First microwave radiometer flown to lunar orbit (channels at 3.0, 7.8, 19.35 and 37 GHz); produced the first microwave map covering the entire lunar surface

facts.label: Full-Moon map
facts.value: China's first map of the entire lunar surface, published 12 November 2008, from stereo camera coverage acquired November 2007 to July 2008

facts.label: ESA tracking support
facts.value: ESA's ESTRACK stations at Maspalomas, Kourou and New Norcia tracked Chang'e 1 from 1 November 2007, through translunar flight and the orbit-insertion burns, covering stretches when China's own stations could not see the spacecraft

facts.label: Mission cost
facts.value: 1.4 billion yuan, about 180 million dollars at the time

facts.label: Data returned
facts.value: 1.37 TB of raw science data, processed into about 4 TB of standard data products

facts.label: Controlled impact
facts.value: 1 March 2009, 08:13 UTC, in Mare Fecunditatis; braking began at 07:36 UTC on commands from the Qingdao and Kashi stations; announced coordinates 1.50 S, 52.36 E; described by China's space administration as planned and controlled, to bank experience for the landing phase

facts.label: Impact site identified
facts.value: A fan of bright ejecta at 1.66 S, 52.27 E, spraying past a 15 m crater that is probably pre-existing, found by Phil Stooke by comparing a 1972 Apollo 16 panoramic-camera frame with LROC images; about 4.4 km from the trajectory-based prediction (published in Icarus, 2019)

timeline: Jan 2004
First phase of the Chang'e program, the lunar orbiter, is formally approved, opening China's lunar exploration effort
Launch at 10:05 UTC on a Long March 3A from Xichang Satellite Launch Center
Trans-lunar injection after a week of phasing-orbit burns around Earth
Lunar orbit insertion: China's first spacecraft in orbit around another world
Third braking burn settles the orbiter into its 200 km, 127-minute circular polar working orbit
CCD stereo camera shoots the 19 frames of China's first lunar image, highlands near Mare Australe
Premier Wen Jiabao unveils the first image at the Beijing Aerospace Control Center
China publishes its first map of the entire lunar surface, built from a year of stereo camera coverage
Orbit lowered from 200 km to 100 km
Perilune dropped to 15 km, rehearsing the low passes later landing missions would need
Controlled impact in Mare Fecunditatis at 08:13 UTC, commanded through the Qingdao and Kashi stations
Chang'e 2, built from Chang'e 1's backup spacecraft with technical improvements, launches from Xichang
Feb 2017
Phil Stooke identifies the impact scar in LROC images, an ejecta fan at 1.66 S, 52.27 E; the identification is published in Icarus in 2019
